title: Save the World by Saving Your Own Mind
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Here's a summary paragraph summarizing the main teaching of the Soto Zen dharma talk: The true essence of Zen lies not in meditation alone, but in embracing a holistic approach that integrates wisdom, conduct, community, intellectual exploration, and personal reflection into daily life. By doing so, one can cultivate a deeper sense of wonder, awe, and connection with others, leading to a more balanced and compassionate self. Ultimately, this approach allows us to live with greater ease, love, and peace, even in the midst of suffering, by embracing the present moment and letting go of attachments to specific outcomes.

sentences.text: Everybody knows what the word zen means.
It means meditation.
It's the way the Japanese pronounce the Chinese chan.
And the Chinese were transliterating jhana, or jhana from Sanskrit, so they read it as chan.

Because the Chinese used transliteration, Chinese people have a hard time reading Buddhist texts because they sound like complete outlandish gibberish: they used characters that sounded like the characters but meant something completely different.
So if you read a Chinese Buddhist text, a Chinese person says, what?
But if you know the transliterations, it makes sense.
Anyway, chan, jhana, chan, zen, tian in Vietnamese, son in Korean, meditation.
So naturally, you would think that zen would be the school of Buddhism that most emphasizes meditation.
But I don't think so.
I think the reason that zen is called zen is not because it emphasizes meditation, but because it radically redefines meditation.
Remember all the million zen stories about how meditation is useless, like the one Tim brought up, I think, on the first day, polishing the tile.
You can't make a mirror by polishing a tile.
Well, you can't make a Buddha by doing zazen.
There's a million stories like this in zen.
So they're telling us that the practice is really about something else.
The sixth ancestor, Huineng, who sets the tone for the zen school, says in his platform sutra something like, meditation isn't meditation.
It's really wisdom.
So dhyana is really prajna.
Meditation isn't just sitting and breathing to purify the mind and get enlightenment.
Meditation is by itself what is transcendent wisdom.
So wisdom is meditation.
And you don't need zendos to practice that.
You can practice that anytime.
And the story of Huineng illustrates that because he becomes the sixth zen ancestor without ever going into the zendo.
He spends the whole time pounding rice in the pantry and doesn't ever go into the zendo because he's not invited.
He's just a functionary, like a worker in the monastery.
So even though we think that we've been meditating this week and that meditation, zazen, is our practice, actually the more we meditate, the more we see that everything is our practice.
Life is actually our practice.
And the reason why we're practicing meditation is to express that and to enhance our appreciation of it and to enjoy its awesomeness.
And Dogen says this very clearly in Fukanzazengi.
He says zazen is not a matter of sitting or anything like that.
It's not a matter of what posture you're in.
And zazen is not meditation, he says.
It's not meditation.
It's the dharma gate of repose and bliss.
So there are a lot of ways of understanding this teaching.
One way you could say it is that our practice is mostly about precepts.
And to practice zazen is to practice precepts, meaning conduct, the way we live.
All our acts of body, speech, and mind are our practice.
And zazen is perfect precept practice.
You're not hurting anybody when you're sitting zazen.
You're totally non-aggressive, right?
Not speaking about the faults of others or anything like that.
And you're sitting there in perfect accord with all existence, in perfect harmony with all sentient beings in zazen.
And when we sit, we open our hearts.
Also Tim mentioned this.
We're creating space inside so that we can more deeply feel our caring and our love.
And the more deeply we feel it and the more often we return to that feeling, the more natural it becomes for us to shape our thoughts, our words, and our deeds around those feelings.
So it's not to say that zazen is not important.
It is important, but it's not important in the way we might have thought it was in the beginning.
Now we understand zazen practice is a whole life.
Now we have a huge meditation movement all over the Western world.
And it emphasizes brain science and all the physical and emotional benefits of meditation.
And the implication of this might be that meditation is pretty much the equivalent of a medication.
Take two of these and call me in the morning.
I think you'll be better.
Your brain is going to change.
Your physiology is going to change.
And to be sure, this is not a religion.
And there is no need whatsoever for all the stupid religious trappings, which are after all just some cultural baggage from another time and place that we can easily dispense with.
Because this medication, I mean meditation, is rational and scientific and completely independent of any Buddhist context.
But the truth is that there's no such thing as anything that's independent of context, including you and me.
So the contemporary secular meditation movement is giving us another context rather than the original context.

And this context is very good because it creates the possibility for people who would never dream of bowing or hanging around with Buddhist statues to take up a very beneficial practice that they otherwise would never do.
So this is a good thing.
But for us, our practice is not just the medication.
I mean meditation.
It really is a whole life.
It's ritual.
Everything in sesshin is ritualized.
And ritual gives you a feeling.
Do it enough and overcome your distaste for it, if you have a distaste for it, and eventually you get a feeling of wonder and awe and timelessness.
You get a feeling that you really belong to an ancient past and you belong to others.
So zen practice is also ritual.
It's also community, deep friendship over time, which includes relationships to teachers and senior students who you look up to and who guide you.
It also has an intellectual component because we're studying the Dharma.
Decades and decades of Dharma study.
I don't mean take exams or something, but we're listening to Dharma talks and naturally we're interested in the Dharma.
So we follow our interest and we study and we read and we discuss.

And little by little we come to appreciate the Dharma view and we integrate the Dharma view into the view that we already had, which was in many ways a limited view and an imprisoning view and a view that blinded us perhaps to some really important things that we just weren't seeing because of the view that we had.
Zen practice especially includes our own thoughts and reflections and observations over a lifetime as we think and speak and feel and share our lives with others.
Years ago, Tricycle Magazine used to sponsor a Buddhist picnic in the park in New York where they called it Change Your Mind Day.
Yeah, maybe they still do it.
Do they still do it?
Yeah, I'm pretty out of touch with Tricycle Magazine, but yeah, they still do it.
Good.
It was really fun.
So maybe they're still having fun.
The people would bring food.
If you're lucky, the weather was good.
People bring food, spread out a blanket, and they raise a little platform and there are different Buddhist teachers giving little short teachings and practices and stuff.
It was really fun.
So how do you do this?
How do you change your mind?
Well, your mind changes by itself, right?
The mind you have now isn't the same mind you had when you were five years old, for sure.
It isn't the same mind you had 10 or 20 or 30 years ago.
So your mind has changed.
Your mind is changing all the time, like everything, because the various conditions that produce this moment of your mind have been developing all along.
So naturally, your mind is changing according to conditions, the experiences of your lifetime, including the historical moment in which you live.
Generally, not necessarily anyway, for the better, but perhaps maybe for the better.
So practice in all the many aspects that I've just been talking about is a mind-changing condition.
When you practice, you have a greater capacity for balanced self-reflection, and practicing zazen certainly helps with this.
There's just more space in your mind.
I mean, we're all smart people.
We don't need zazen to help us think, but zazen creates space sort of in between the thoughts and it helps you to see the thoughts and feelings arising.
And also, it sensitizes you to yourself so that you can see the character of your thoughts.
And lots of zazen over time shows you how to be patient with your thoughts.
Because you realize, after all, they're just thoughts.
They're not yours and they're not your fault.

And you learn how to tell the difference between thoughts that seem compelling, but actually make you miserable, so you can, in fact, drop them, and other thoughts that are wholesome and happy thoughts and can be encouraged.
So as you practice and reflect and hear the Dharma again and again, you test all this out with your own experience.
And you develop your own sort of unique inner culture, because your thoughts are not the same as the next guy's thoughts and your emotions are not the same as the next person's.

So little by little, through practicing Dharma and reflection, you find your own inner culture, a sense of how to live with your unique mind so as to maximize your love and ease and minimize your craziness and your suffering.
And you understand very well that the mind is always subject to conditions.
And this is a very, very humbling thought.
What it means is that when the conditions for suffering are present, the mind will experience suffering, just the way it is.
If all of a sudden you feel a strong pain in your body, you will suffer.
If all of a sudden you lose someone that you love, you will experience suffering.
Because that's what happens when you have a human mind, when you have a body, and when you're lucky enough to love someone.
But when you have an inner culture of practice, you know this and you accept it.
And in accepting it and allowing yourself to suffer as you must, you can suffer appropriately without thinking somehow that you're supposed to be beyond suffering or be able to fix all problems.
And when you know that and you practice that way, you can actually reduce the suffering.
It's okay to suffer, but it's not okay to unwisely make it worse, basically.
To flail around and jump up and down and start throwing things around the room and hitting other people with them, and they bounce back and hit you.
Don't do that.
And you know how not to do that.
You know how not to do it.
And sometimes you do it, naturally.
Because sometimes you can't help it.
You do it anyway.
And then you know what you're doing.
And you just know you have to find a way to stop yourself.
Or maybe a good friend will stop you.
And then you have to think and you have to get a grip.
Maybe you sit or you walk or you just stand there.
You do what you can to remind yourself that some suffering is okay, but too much suffering is going too far.
And so you accept what's happening and you know there's a reason for it.
And you sometimes claw your way back to your breath, to your body.
And you will calm down.
Because there are precepts and teachings you know and have committed yourself to.
Eventually you will know what to do and you will do it.
And you will know what not to do and you'll forbear.
And you will realize that the pain in your life is your great teacher.
And it will bring forth in you what has been there all along, but long hidden.
And it will be your job to digest this pain and turn it into a Dharma treasure.
And then your ability to understand and love others will be much increased.
And when your mind is not suffering like that, you're paying attention all the time to what arises every day in your heart.
And you're taking care of yourself all the time.
Since you know that practice isn't just on the cushion or in the zendo, you're always alive to your life.
You're paying attention to what you're doing all the time, the best you can.
All walking is kinhin at whatever pace.
All standing is standing meditation.
All sitting is zazen.
Maybe you have a practice like we've been doing this week.
Before you eat, you chant a verse.
Maybe you wash your hands before you eat and chant a verse.
Maybe going to bed, you chant a verse.
Maybe rising up, you chant a verse.
These are all traditional practices in the monastery.
Recently I received a great teaching like this from a rabbi friend of mine.
My usual practice most of the time is to get up in the morning, wash my face and rinse out my mouth, and go out to the zendo, our little zendo, and sit.
But this rabbi was giving a talk and he said, what's the very first thing you do in the morning?
And nobody said anything.
So he said, come on, you look at your phone.
And everybody laughed because most of the people, myself included, I do that.
I mean, I don't like going on and on with the phone, but I look at the phone.
Maybe the world fell down while I was sleeping and I look at the phone.
So I do that.
I glance at the phone.
Then I get up and wash my face.
I don't even know I looked at the phone because I don't even think of that.
I think I wash my face and then I, but no, I actually looked at the phone first.
So the reason the rabbi was saying that, because he was talking about a traditional Jewish prayer that you're supposed to say, theoretically, the moment of unwaking.
You're supposed to say this prayer, moda ani, which means I am grateful.
It's a whole prayer that you say about your gratefulness.
It's wonderful.
Why not remember first thing in the morning, first thing on waking up, how great it is that you're still alive?
You just had a good night's sleep.
You woke up.
You still think you're you.
The world still makes sense, more or less the way it was yesterday.
Why should that be so?
You were totally unconscious.
You could wake up and it could be like another universe.
You'd be totally disoriented and confused.
But no, the world kind of held itself together while you were asleep.
And it's there for you when you wake up.
You got out of bed, so your body still works.
Whoa, you still seem to be yourself, not somebody else.
So there's plenty to be grateful for just in that first moment of being awake.

So I first learned about this beautiful gratefulness practice to do in the morning before anything else from, I'm sure I've spoken about it before, our great Dharma brother, Steve Stuckey, who was doing this practice every morning very poignantly during the last part of his life when he had pancreatic cancer.
And he was suffering terribly.
And every morning he woke up and he practiced gratefulness.
So I thought, I'm going to do that too.
That's great.
I'll do it in memory of Steve.
But I always forget.
I wake up and I stumble out of bed and I go to sit and I forget.
I just totally forgot about it entirely until this rabbi reminded me of it.
So then I realized, well, I use my phone for everything else.
Maybe since I already have this habit of checking my phone automatically, I can use the checking of my phone to remind me to say moda ani.
So ever since that rabbi said that, I've been doing that.
And now I'm remembering because my phone, I look at the phone and say, no, no.
And then I stop and I say that prayer, and I remember gratitude.
So I was already feeling pretty grateful, but now I think maybe a little more gratitude because I say that prayer every day.
It's a great practice.
Anyway, I'm telling you this as just a little example of how all the time we can create ways to remind us of who we really are and how we really want to live.
We create a culture for ourselves of Dharma.
The world is now and has always been a crazy and a difficult place to live in.
And so that's why we need to do all this, so we can cope in this crazy world.
But of course, it's not just the world.
It's us.
Just like Michael Jackson sang years ago, we are the world.
We are the world because the world that we live in literally is the world plus your mind.
So save the world by saving your own mind.
That's what the sixth ancestor says.
We cannot afford not to pay attention to our lives.
So I'm sure I've mentioned before that one of my jobs in life, it would appear, is reading manuscripts.
People give me manuscripts all the time for what I make a little blurb.
So I'm reading a great manuscript, just finished it, by our friend Grace Schurson.
It has quite a provocative title, Naked in the Zendo.
Naked in the Zendo, stories of uptight zen, wild ass zen, and enlightenment wherever you are.
That's the title of it.
Naked in the Zendo, stories of uptight zen, wild ass zen, and enlightenment wherever you are.
And this title is all Grace, that's Grace.
She is an amazing person.
First of all, she's very tall.
Grace is maybe like six foot one or something, a really tall woman.
And she has a personality to match.
You meet Grace, you know you met somebody.
She's a very powerful feminist, but in that subcategory of feminists who love to shop, who are astute and enthusiastic shoppers.
And she loves clothing and fashion.
So when you see Grace, you are going to see one dolled up lady.
You're going to see some pretty good shoes and probably some colorful scarves.
You're going to see a pair of earrings make up the whole works.
She's looking good all the time, Grace.
And seeing her, you might not imagine that she has been a very hardcore Zen student for many, many, many decades.
She's in our Dharma family.
She's our Dharma sister, the disciple of Sojun from Berkeley Zen Center.
That's been her Dharma home since she was young.
But astonishingly enough, she has also practiced in Japan.
She made trips to Japan, lengthy trips every year for decades, or maybe 10, 15 years anyway.
And she studied Koan Zen in a hardcore all-male Zen monastery with a tough Japanese Roshi.
So this is Grace.
She's amazing.
And in her book, she tells you the story of her first ever encounter with Suzuki Roshi when she was a young girl.
This by now is its own literary genre.
First encounters with Suzuki Roshi is like a whole branch of literature by now.
But this is a particularly great story, so I'm going to read you from Grace's book.
I guess at this time she's maybe 18 or something like that.
*So my sister and I rode our motorcycles across the Bay Bridge from Berkeley to San Francisco on our psychedelic quest.
We made a brief stop at an import store to further decorate ourselves with large hoop earrings.
And we were well made up.
I wore a miniskirt, tights, and shoes similar to those worn by Dorothy in The Wizard of Oz, and a necklace with bells that jingled when I walked.
And so we appeared to an amused Suzuki Roshi who answered our apprehensive knock at the Zen center's front door.
Suzuki Roshi knew who we were and why we had come before we said a word.*
I wonder how he knew.
I guess it was like Zen master intuition or something.
Anyway, she says he knew.
And he had been teaching Zen to hippies in San Francisco already by then for a decade, so he knew who he was dealing with.
*And part of the hippie credo was an abundant confidence in our worldview.
And I was imbued with the belief that I had the most profound worldview ever to be known by a living being.
And so we entered the world of Zen.
Without ceremony, Suzuki Roshi led us upstairs to the Zendo meditation space.
He showed us to the meditation tatami platform and motioned us over to the black round and rectangular cushion, the zafus and zabatans, perfectly spaced with yellow woven tatami mats.
And the sight of this orderly clean space sent a wave of aesthetic appreciation through my mind.
Was this how you got high?
He instructed us to bow to the cushion and bow away and explained that we needed to do this because we needed to bow to the spirits sitting on the cushion.
Because when we took our places to meditate, we would be displacing them.*
*And I was so excited about how far out this little old man was.
And I was really looking forward to meeting these meditating spirits and their mysterious power to get me high.
But instead of meeting the invisible spirits, I received my first zazen instruction.
And we spent what appeared like to us two hours meditating with him for the next 10 minutes.
The discomfort in my undisciplined mind was running away with me.
Would this work?
Would I get high?
What was taking so long?
I was able to put aside my discomfort because I knew that the goodies and the high were coming soon.
So when we finished our meditation, we turned towards Suzuki Roshi for our personal map to getting high.
And he knew that he had our full attention.
And although his English was poor, I have a feeling that he made it even worse to ensure that we listen carefully.
And so we hung on every word.
And he began with words that promised us our place in the high zone, the ticket to getting high from Zen.
He said, the more*, and he had a very quiet voice.
*He said, the more you, the more you know, the more you realize, the more you know that, and he concluded, the more you know that life is suffering.
We were stunned.
Suffering?
The more you practice Zen, the more you realize that life is suffering?*
*We were so horrified that we didn't even have time to think about what happened.
It never occurred to us in our pursuit of getting high that this might actually be another religion like Catholicism or Judaism.
We thought Zen was so cool.
But was it a religion like those from which we'd run away?
After Suzuki Roshi's pronouncement, all we could manage was getting out of the Zen center as fast as we could.
I doubt we even said thank you and goodbye.*
So as you see, she's a good storyteller, and she has many fascinating stories.
Her stories about her practice in Japan are really wonderful.
And sometimes she brings up classical Zen stories like case 86 from the Blue Cliff Record.
Here's the story, case 86.
*Yunmun imparted some words, saying, everyone has a light.
When you look at it, you don't see it, and it's dark and dim.
What is everybody's light?
And he answered himself on their behalf, the kitchen pantry and the main gate.
He also said, a good thing isn't as good as nothing.*
So this is a great story, and it's worth remembering these words of Yunmun.
Everyone has a light.
When you look for it, you don't see it.
It's dark, and a good thing isn't as good as nothing.
You have a light.
I have a light.
This light has been here from the beginning, and the whole time it's been guiding us and protecting us.
Even when it looks like we're sinking, and we're almost sunk, the light is still there taking care of us.
When we try to find it, when we try to see it, it looks like darkness, because it is darkness.
You can't see it.
Maybe the whole point of our practice is just to know for sure that this light is there, and to have confidence in it.
And then when we have confidence in it, we know that whatever happens, we can trust our life.
We can trust what happens to us.
Of course, if you secretly have an aspiration, an impulse, a desire that such and so will happen, and that the light is going to make sure that such and so is going to happen, you'll be disappointed.
Because even if such and so actually does happen, just as you planned, like we heard the other day, it won't be satisfactory.
It won't help you, because you won't be there for it.
That's why Yunmun adds, a good thing isn't as good as nothing.
What is this light?
We must keep asking.
If we stop asking, we become arrogant and confused, and we'll just suffer all over again.
What is this light?
Where is this light?
The kitchen pantry and the main gate, the bathroom, the car, the airport, the shopping mall.
Xuedou's poem on the case, I won't read it for you, but I'll just read the last line, which is to me the best line and the only line we need.
He says,
*Riding backwards on an ox, entering the Buddhist shrine.*
The ox is the mind.
It pulls and hauls for you, and you can use its dung to heat your house in the winter.
But first, it's time to tame it.
When you ride the ox backwards, it means you have confidence in the mind and in things as they are, just as they are.
In other words, you're not riding the ox forward this way, grabbing for something ahead of you.

You're riding it backwards, here where you are, turning the mind around, taking the backward step, not looking for something, not pushing forth, not pushing out [unclear: "some scars"] toward a desired future, but looking within, letting go right here in this moment.
And when you ride the ox backwards, the line says, you are entering the Buddhist shrine, and that's your home.
So I'll share with you Grace's commentary to this case, which is quite wonderful.
*In case 86 of the Blue Cliff Record, Yun Mun said, everyone has their own light.
If you look for it, you can't find it.
In other words, the light can illuminate your mind, but with an idea in your mind that you will get this light, it doesn't appear.
When you are after something, you create a mindset of activity, of mental commotion, a separated self that is looking for something.
One part of your mind has separated and is chasing after a prized goal, just like a dog chasing his own tail.
Lots of activity, but no goal accomplished.
It's like creating ripples when reaching for a stick in the water.
What you're trying to reach gets further away.
And that's why children can have a spontaneous experience of the mind lighting up and expanding, because they're not yet trying to achieve anything in particular.
Actually, the light appears on its own when you become rather than pursue a unified presence.
And that's why Yun Mun cautioned against seeking it.
When you settle into your own being, your own breath, your own body, when you unite body, breath, and mind, you connect with yourself.
Naturally, your mind reflects the light of awareness.
And this light allows you to watch your own thoughts as they arise through finding spaciousness, light, or luminosity in your mind.
You can observe the subtle movements of the mind without being pulled around to act on them.
You enjoy a sense of grounded connection while just watching what arises in your mind.
No grasping, no averting.
You develop an unfiltered intimacy with what is actually going through your mind and to the circumstances to which your mind is reacting.*
Isn't that a wonderful commentary?
So I'm told that today is the last day of our sesshin.
Is this a surprise?
Yeah, that's what they told me.
That this is the last day of our sesshin and not that long from now we'll all be returning to our homes far and near.
What happened?
What can we report to our friends?
Not that much.
I think we've all said enough to make it clear that there's no use expecting any benefits at all from sesshins.
The only thing you can do is go home and take care of things as they arise the best you can, enduring, once again, the disturbed and complicated world.
There is no way to shut the world out and there is no way to live in the world without being affected by it.
And of course, we want to be affected by the world.
We want to be moved by the world to tears and laughter.
But we do not need to be overcome, because now we know that the world is not the world.
The world is, as I said, the world plus our mind.
And how we see and live in this world is up to us.
Lots of people these days think the world is worse off than ever because of that.
That's why I wrote the world could be otherwise, because I'm aware that so many of my friends think the world is worse off now than it's ever been.
Or maybe at least it seems like worse off than it was when we were young, which maybe is true.
Maybe not.
It's kind of hard to tell.
But I think we all probably would agree that we have serious social and political troubles.
And at this moment, it's hard to see a leader or a party or a cause that seems promising enough to raise our spirits enough to make us happy, give us hope.
And on top of it all, we have a pretty terrible environmental problem.
I think we're all worried about this.
We don't know the exact details or precisely what's going to happen, but we know enough to be reasonably upset.
And it seems that so far we haven't really done anything about it.
Nothing, really.
And plus we keep putting more of the stuff in the atmosphere that causes the trouble.
We're not even reducing the amount of stuff that we're putting.
So who could complain if someone feels despair, guilt, anger, and so on?
But actually, that doesn't make sense.
That's extra.
It's understandable, but it really is not reasonable.
And I give myself as an example.
I've been saying this to people, to explain.
Consider my case.
I personally am entirely doomed, right?
I'm doomed.
It is 100% certain that in a fairly short amount of time, something bad is going to happen to me, right?
I'll either get sick and die, or I'll be really, really old and nothing will work.

But oddly enough, I'm quite grateful, as I said before, for my life.
I'm a very happy person.
I'm sure that I'm much happier now than I was when I had more reason to be happy than I do now.
I'm more amazed at being alive than I ever have been.

Oh, no.

In my life, I am always grieving for someone.

So my life is very happy and very sad all the time.
And this is wonderful because it reminds me of how precious my life is and how much I care.
So that's the example I'm using to say, why don't we do this together like this?
If we're doomed, right?
Like I'm doomed.
